hook.line: Tomás has just waited three hours at a clinic, and moaning "I waited three hours" feels too personal. Spanish speakers turn it into something that happens to anyone.
hook.es: En esa clínica llegas y te toca esperar tres horas.
hook.en: At that clinic you show up and have to wait three hours.

examples.es: En esa clínica llegas y te toca esperar tres horas.
examples.en: At that clinic you show up and have to wait three hours.

examples.es: Cuando uno está cansado, todo le molesta.
examples.en: When you're tired, everything bothers you.

examples.es: Trabajas todo el día y al final no te alcanza la plata.

examples.es: Sales a las seis y te toca esperar el bus una hora.
examples.en: You leave at six and have to wait an hour for the bus.

rule:
When you talk about your own experience, you can turn it into something that happens to anyone. Spanish has two ways.

*Tú* with no one in particular: *Llegas y te toca esperar.* English does the same with "you".

*Uno* + the *él* form: *Uno hace lo que puede.* Think "one", but it is common and relaxed in Spanish. With *uno* the pronoun is *le*, not *te*: *todo le molesta*.

*Te toca* + infinitive means "it falls to you to": the thing you have to do, usually a nuisance. It is very natural in Latin America.

The speaker is often really talking about themselves. The "anyone" protects them from sounding like they are complaining.
smallPrint: Teachers call this generic or impersonal *tú* and the impersonal use of *uno*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *te toca* or *te tocan*: Llegas a la notaría y ___ esperar mucho. Type the whole sentence.
yourTurn.answer: Llegas a la notaría y te toca esperar mucho.
yourTurn.why: *Toca* goes with an infinitive (one thing to do), so it stays singular.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish (anyone, in general): You do what you can.
Type in Spanish (anyone, in general): You work all day and the money isn't enough.
yourTurn.answer: Trabajas todo el día y no te alcanza la plata.
accept: Trabajas todo el día y al final no te alcanza la plata.
yourTurn.why: *Tú* with no one in particular, and *no te alcanza* for "isn't enough for you".

yourTurn.prompt: Say it about anyone, with *uno*: *Cuando estoy cansado, todo me molesta.*
yourTurn.answer: Cuando uno está cansado, todo le molesta.
yourTurn.why: With *uno* the verb is *está* and the pronoun is *le*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it with generic *tú*: *Aquí uno aprende rápido.*
yourTurn.why: *Uno* takes the *él* form; generic *tú* takes the *tú* form.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish (anyone, in general): At that clinic you show up and have to wait three hours.
yourTurn.answer: En esa clínica llegas y te toca esperar tres horas.
yourTurn.why: *Te toca* + infinitive is the nuisance that falls to you.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish (anyone, in general): Here you never know.

pitfalls.why: Almost. *Uno* is a third-person word, so the verb is *puede*, not the *yo* form.

pitfalls.wrong: Cuando uno está cansado, todo te molesta.
pitfalls.right: Cuando uno está cansado, todo le molesta.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Te* belongs with *tú*; with *uno* the matching pronoun is *le*.

pitfalls.wrong: Tú trabajas todo el día y no te alcanza la plata.
pitfalls.right: Trabajas todo el día y no te alcanza la plata.
pitfalls.why: Almost. Saying *tú* points at the listener; leave it out and "you" means anyone.

personal: Choose something that annoys you about your city. Say it as if it happens to everyone, with *uno* or generic *tú*.
